analysis.one_liner: Extends the 36% interest-rate cap now given to service members to all borrowers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced September 16, 2026 with one cosponsor, has sat in the House Financial Services Committee since the day it was introduced, with no hearing or floor vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: Members of the military already get special protection when they borrow: under the Military Lending Act, lenders cannot charge them more than a 36% annual percentage rate once fees are counted, and cannot use harsh terms like prepayment penalties. This bill would write those same rules into the Truth in Lending Act and apply them to every American consumer, not just service members and their families. It would chiefly change the market for high-cost small-dollar loans — payday, title, and subprime installment lending — and high-rate credit card accounts.
analysis.who_benefits: All consumer borrowers, especially households with low incomes or weak credit who are most likely to take out payday, title, and other high-cost loans and pay rates far above 36%. The bill would also stop lenders from charging the fees and penalty structures that are banned for military borrowers [S1].

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends the consumer credit protections that service members and their dependents currently receive under title 10 federal law to all consumers under the Truth in Lending Act [S1].

For military families, those protections mean lenders cannot charge more than a 36% annual percentage rate once fees are included, and cannot impose terms such as prepayment penalties or automatic account access; the bill would give every borrower the same shield [S1].

Because the cap applies to the total cost of credit, it targets the loans where rates most often run to triple digits — short-term payday and title loans and subprime installment credit — where households with the least money pay the most.

analysis.who_pays: High-cost lenders — payday, auto-title, subprime installment, and deposit-advance lenders — whose business model depends on rates above 36%, plus credit card issuers whose subprime and penalty rates exceed the cap. Some borrowers with very poor credit may lose access to those loans if lenders decline to serve them at a capped rate.

drawbacks.text: A blanket rate cap can cut off supply, not just cut prices: lenders that cannot price for risk above 36% may simply stop lending to the weakest borrowers, leaving some people with no loan option at all instead of an expensive one [S1].

Borrowers who lose access to capped-out loans may turn to worse alternatives — unregulated lenders, overdrafts, or late fees on bills — so the bill's net effect depends on how many lenders exit the market rather than adjust to it [S1].

Most prime credit card rates are already below 36%, so for many cardholders little changes, while the cost falls hardest on lenders serving customers with the poorest credit — who are the same customers the bill is trying to protect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and real for the households that currently pay triple-digit rates on small loans, and the 36% cap is a tested rule — the military version has been in effect since 2006. The honest cost is that some high-risk borrowers could lose a loan option they used before; a fair weighing turns on whether cheaper alternatives (credit unions, employer-based lending, bank small-dollar products) fill the gap. The bill does not include a replacement-credit plan, so that risk is real but is also the standard objection to every rate cap.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on September 16, 2026 [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, and the action record shows nothing further [S3].
The bill has one cosponsor, a Democrat, in addition to its Republican sponsor [S2].
With the 119th Congress scheduled to end January 3, 2027, the bill has roughly three and a half months in which to move, and its committee has taken no action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened yet, the main beneficiaries of the current situation are high-cost lenders, who continue to operate under the existing rate rules while service members keep protections other borrowers lack. Borrowers who would have gained from a national rate cap have gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Glenn Grothman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Financial Services Committee.

against.name: French Hill
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the record shows no committee action since the day of referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only backers are a conservative Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — a bipartisan pair, but too few members to say anything about how the parties line up; there have been no votes.

industries.industry: Payday, auto-title, and subprime installment lenders
industries.note: These lenders' core product is small-dollar credit priced above 36% APR; the bill would make that illegal nationwide, as it already is for loans to service members. Ordinary borrowers in this market would gain the most if cheaper lenders fill the gap these firms left.

Prime card rates are mostly below 36% and would be untouched, but subprime card rates and penalty rates above 36% would be capped. Issuers would lose revenue from the highest-rate accounts — the accounts held by the most financially stretched cardholders.

industries.industry: Banks and credit unions offering small-dollar loans
industries.note: Institutions that already make loans at or under 36% would face no new constraint and could gain customers if high-cost lenders exit. Military-family lending by credit unions shows this model exists.

analysis.trajectory: Very unlikely to become law in this Congress. The bill was introduced in mid-September 2026 with a single cosponsor, has no committee hearing on the record, and would need committee action, a House floor vote, and Senate action all within about three and a half months. Most bills at this stage and with this level of support die when the Congress ends.
